details:
PROJECT REPORT: LOST, BUT NOT FORGOTTEN

Interactive Bilingual Educational Web Application on Robotic Space Exploration

1. General Project Summary

·       What is the project about? “Space Explorers: The Moon and Mars” (Kids Space Adventure) is an educational, interactive, and bilingual (English and Spanish) web application designed with a kid-friendly aesthetic. Its purpose is to teach children and young learners about real space probes, rovers, landers, and space telescopes sent to The Moon, Mars, and Deep Space, organizing the information into 13 individual sections (4 lunar and 9 Martian/deep-space) with visual cards and three fundamental questions per mission.

·       Why is it important? Early science outreach often presents barriers such as complex technical language or excessive text that discourage young audiences. This project translates historical and scientific milestones of space exploration into clear, visual, and accessible concepts, fostering curiosity in Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) from an early age while removing language barriers through a built-in instant translator.

·       How was the challenge addressed? A responsive single-page web interface was designed with intuitive three-level navigation: (1) a home screen with visual selection between The Moon and Planet Mars, (2) direct-access themed grids (4 cards for The Moon and 9 cards for Mars), and (3) a dedicated individual view for each mission featuring original vector illustrations and structured answers to three key questions: What are they?, Why were they sent?, and What discoveries did they make and what are they doing right now?

Demonstration Format

3. Technical and Functional Project Details

3.1 What does it do exactly?

The application works as an interactive space encyclopedia divided into two main explorable worlds. Upon entering, the user sees an animated starry space environment and two main illustrated buttons: “The Moon” (4 sections) and “Planet Mars” (9 sections). Selecting any card opens an individual view dedicated exclusively to that space mission, displaying its vector illustration and answering three educational questions in simple terms: what the spacecraft or artifact is, why it was sent, and what discoveries it made or what its current status is. Additionally, it includes a top translator button that toggles the entire interface and educational texts between English and Spanish without losing the current screen.

3.2 How does it work? (Architecture and Navigation Flow)

·       Client-side state management: Uses a centralized JavaScript object (state) that tracks the active language (lang: 'en' | 'es'), current view (view: 'home' | 'grid' | 'detail'), selected planet, and mission identifier.

·       Dynamic DOM rendering: The functions render(), openPlanet(), openItem(), and toggleLanguage() dynamically rebuild the views inside the main container (#app) without reloading the page, ensuring smooth transitions with CSS animations (animate-pop and animate-float).

·       Embedded vector graphics (SVG): All illustrations of planets, rovers, landers, helicopters, and telescopes are coded as Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG_ART) directly inside the source code, eliminating external image dependencies and ensuring crisp visuals on any screen.

3.2 How does it work? (Architecture and Navigation Flow)

·       Client-side state management: Uses a centralized JavaScript object (state) that tracks the active language (lang: 'en' | 'es'), current view (view: 'home' | 'grid' | 'detail'), selected planet, and mission identifier.

·       Dynamic DOM rendering: The functions render(), openPlanet(), openItem(), and toggleLanguage() dynamically rebuild the views inside the main container (#app) without reloading the page, ensuring smooth transitions with CSS animations (animate-pop and animate-float).

·       Embedded vector graphics (SVG): All illustrations of planets, rovers, landers, helicopters, and telescopes are coded as Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG_ART) directly inside the source code, eliminating external image dependencies and ensuring crisp visuals on any screen.

3.4 What benefits does it have and what does it aim to achieve?

·       Educational and accessibility benefits: Promotes scientific literacy in children, supports bilingual English-Spanish learning of space vocabulary, runs without installation on any mobile or desktop browser, and maintains ultra-fast loading.

·       Future goals (what it aims to achieve): Spark early scientific interest in boys and girls, serve as an open educational resource for elementary school classrooms, and scale the platform by adding Text-to-Speech voice narration, interactive quizzes, and new solar system bodies.

3.5 Tools, Languages, and Technologies Used

·       Standard web languages: Semantic HTML5, modern CSS3 (custom @keyframes animations, radial gradients), and JavaScript (ES6+) for navigation logic, dynamic rendering, and bilingual translation.

·       Frameworks and typography: Tailwind CSS (via CDN) for responsive design and adaptive grid layouts; Google Fonts (“Fredoka” for friendly titles and “Nunito” for clear readability).

·       Vector graphics: SVG (Scalable Vector Graphics) coded directly in HTML/JS for all kid-friendly space illustrations.

·       Software and development environment: Web source code editor, modern browser for responsive testing, and Artificial Intelligence assistance tools for pedagogical structuring and synthesis.

4. Use of Artificial Intelligence and NASA Data

·       Use of NASA scientific data: The informational content of the 13 missions is based on public historical and scientific records from NASA regarding the Apollo program (Lunar Modules, LRV, and ALSEP packages), the Surveyor program, Martian rovers (Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity), landers (Viking 1 and 2, Phoenix, InSight), the Ingenuity helicopter, as well as the Dawn, NEAR Shoemaker, Pioneer 10/11, and Kepler Space Telescope missions (https://science.nasa.gov/missions/).

·       Use of Artificial Intelligence tools: Generative Artificial Intelligence models were used to support three specific areas: (1) pedagogical synthesis and adaptation of technical mission data into child-friendly language in English and Spanish, (2) creation of original kid-friendly SVG vector illustrations, and (3) optimization of the JavaScript navigation architecture.

·       Strict compliance with NASA branding policies: In strict adherence to hackathon guidelines and NASA media usage rules, the web application does NOT use, contain, or modify any official NASA logos (neither the “meatball” insignia nor the “worm” logotype), institutional flags, or official mission graphic identifiers. All visual elements were created as original kid-friendly vector illustrations.

5. References and Resources Used
